newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels offer truce, Mobutu flies to France.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels offer truce, Mobutu flies to France.

text.p: A ceasefire announced by Tutsi rebels in eastern Zaire on Monday appeared to be holding after a two-week offensive uprooted many of more than a million refugees with little food or water.
At the same time France and Spain said they wanted the idea of a multi-national force to be considered in order to guarantee distribution of humanitarian aid to refugees in Zaire

French President Jacques Chirac and Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar agreed at a summit in the French Mediterranean port of Marseille to "unite their efforts" and prepare a "temporary effort to ensure security" in eastern Zaire.

"The two countries will take part in an international meeting to prepare this operation to which they are prepared to contribute and which should be decided by the U.N. Security Council," the two said in a statement.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said: "What we're proposing is that the international community -- Europe, the United States, African states -- organise so that there is a security force on the ground to guarantee people's safety."
Zaire's ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko left Switzerland after three months in Lausanne, where he was operated on for cancer, and flew to the French Riviera capital of Nice.
His spokesman said on Zaire television that Mobutu was expected to return home shortly, having completed his followup treatment at the end of last month.

Tutsi rebels earlier warned war would resume unless Zaire's army abided by the truce -- a tall order for the military which has vowed to recapture the towns and cities it lost. There was no immediate official Zairean comment on the ceasefire offer.

Zaire reiterated its rejection of talks "while part of its territory is occupied by the aggressor," state radio said, referring to Rwanda which is accused by Zaire of backing Tutsi rebels battling its army.
Interior Minister Kamanda wa Kamanda told Reuters Zaire would not attend regional talks called by Kenya for Tuesday to dael with the crisis.
Asked about the ceasefire, he said: "I am not aware of that."
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said his fighters would observe a three-week ceasefire from 5 p.m. (1500 GMT) to allow 1.1 million Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees to return home.

Reuters correspondent Christian Jennings in the Rwandan border town of Gisenyi bordering on the Zairean city of Goma said on Monday night the ceasefire appeared to be holding as there had been no sounds of gunfire heard since mid-morning.
Fierce battles forced all foreign aid workers on Saturday to flee into Rwanda from Goma, capital of North Kivu province.
"The Alliance for Democracy following a unilateral decision will have a ceasefire to start at 5 p.m. today for three weeks," said Kabila, 56, who has been long a thorn in Mobutu's side.
"This is because of the disquiet of the international community, to allow the International Red Cross to evacuate the refugees who want to return to their original countries."

"We hope that the unilateral ceasefire will be respected by the Zairean side. If they are against this decision, then combat will restart immediately," added Kabila, who called journalists abroad and said he was speaking from the Zairean city of Bukavu.
